subject: Agriculture
title: Feed Conversion Ratios
description: A short lesson to help you apply Feed Conversion Ratios.

hook.text: It takes 8 kg of feed to produce 1 kg of beef—but only 2 kg of feed for 1 kg of chicken.

buildup.text: Feed conversion ratio measures how efficiently an animal turns plant calories into meat calories.

discovery.text: Chickens convert feed to meat four times more efficiently than cattle. Pigs fall in between.

twist.text: Fish are even better—some species achieve 1.2:1 ratios. Cold blood means less energy wasted on body heat.

climax.text: These ratios explain why chicken is cheap and beef expensive—and why aquaculture is booming.

punchline.text: The most efficient meat animal is one that doesn't waste energy staying warm.

quiz.question: Why are fish more feed-efficient than cattle?
options: Being cold-blooded, they waste less energy on body heat

details.summary: Feed conversion ratio measures how efficiently livestock convert feed into meat, milk, or eggs. This topic compares ratios across species, explains why poultry and fish are far more efficient than cattle, and discusses the implications for sustainable food systems.
details.whyItMatters: A chicken needs about 2 kg of feed per kg of meat gained, while a cow needs 6–8 kg. These ratios fundamentally shape the environmental footprint and economics of different animal protein sources.
takeaways: Broiler chickens have the best FCR among land animals at roughly 1.6:1 to 2:1
Cattle have the worst FCR at approximately 6:1 to 8:1 for beef production
Farmed fish like tilapia achieve FCRs of 1.2:1 to 1.5:1, better than any land animal

faq.question: What is a feed conversion ratio?
faq.answer: Feed conversion ratio (FCR) is the weight of feed required to produce one unit of weight gain in an animal. An FCR of 2:1 means 2 kilograms of feed produces 1 kilogram of body weight. Lower ratios indicate more efficient conversion.

faq.question: Why do cattle have such poor feed conversion ratios?
faq.answer: Cattle are large, warm-blooded animals that expend significant energy on maintaining body temperature, movement, and metabolic processes. Their ruminant digestion is designed for grass, not grain, and beef cattle take much longer to reach market weight than poultry.
